Though the climate talks officially finished on Friday, no final deal was agreed. NGOs are warning that this summit might fall disastrously short of what is needed

Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaina Talia, Tuvalu minister for climate change, gives a statement to the media during the first overtime day of the COP31 conference in Antalya, Turkey. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty ImagesAjit Niranjan (now), Natalie Hanman (earlier) and Bibi van der Zee (earlier)Sat 21 Nov 2026 14.23 GMTFirst published on Sat 21 Nov 2026 06.55 GMTShareFrom 7h ago07.26 GMTThis could be one of 'most disappointing Cops' ever, warns civil societyDamien GayleCivil society organisations wrote to Cop31’s joint presidents, Chris Bowen and Murat Kurum, overnight to tell them they had hours left to avoid making it “one of the most disappointing Cops the UNFCCC has ever had”.

“The Global South is being abandoned,” they told the presidencies. “Developed countries have blocked progress across the negotiations and arrived with no new finance commitments.”

The draft cover text “is a gift to the fossil fuel industry”, they went on. “The major cause of the climate crisis – coal, oil and gas – fails to rate a mention.”

Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at COP31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall, where delegates meet during the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) at the Antalya Expo Centre, in Antalya November 20, 2026. Photograph: Yasin Akgül/AFP/Getty ImagesIn sum: “It has all the hallmarks of a deal to let carbon capture through in exchange for an electrification target that does not even require renewables-based electricity or ensures access for the people who need it most. None of this is defensible.”

The letter is co-signed by 100 different environmental organisations, from the Africa Just Transition Network to Zero Waste Alliance Ireland, and including 350.org, Climate Action Network, Greenpeace International and WWF.

They called on the presidencies to remove targets for carbon capture, restore pledges to uphold the rights of indigenous peoples and include measures to make rich countries accountable for public climate finance. They called for the summit to explicitly welcome the advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice that states have a duty to protect the climate.

And they demanded that a link was drawn between the summit’s goal on electrification and the generation of energy from renewable sources and the transition away from fossil fuels.

“Without this link, the target risks supporting additional electricity demand while leaving fossil fuel dependence intact,” the letter said.

“In addition, we ask you to take forward the Cop30 roadmap on transitioning away from fossil fuels, with the Cop30 and Cop32 Presidencies, through to the second Global Stocktake external to the consensus process, as a Presidency-led dialogue.

“Otherwise Ethiopia will unfairly be left to carry the burden of your failure into Cop32.”

We have confirmed that, as far as the Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese is concerned, there have not been any calls from him yet to his counterparts.

Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPShare28m ago14.04 GMTConsensus-driven talks to forge a global treaty with potentially existential consequences for humanity collapsed on Saturday morning. No, not the Cop31 climate summit – we’re still waiting for that outcome. These were UN talks to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons.

View image in fullscreenDelegates at the UN Review Conference of the High Contracting Parties to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) last week. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty ImagesRussia led objections with obstructive stalling tactics, while other countries who have invested heavily in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other such weapons. Among the military powers who wanted only a nonbinding agreement were the UK, France, Germany, South Korea, Japan and Turkey.

Read moreShareUpdated at 14.23 GMT52m ago13.39 GMTFiona HarveyThe main sticking point now is countries, including the EU, small islands and other vulnerable developing nations, trying to get a reference to fossil fuels and the need to transition away from them reinserted in some form into the text. The Guardian has been unable to establish whether the heads of state of the joint presidencies – Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of Turkey and Anthony Albanese of Australia – have made phone calls to their counterparts in foreign capitals, to try to break the impasse.

Pelin Zorlu, senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, told the Guardian: “Erdoğan or Hakan Fidan, Turkey’s foreign minister, calling Saudi will be absolutely necessary to unblock this. Otherwise, there is an increasing probability that Turkey will take the diplomatic blame, as the country that will gavel it through.”

1h ago13.19 GMTFiona HarveyA proposed meeting of the heads of delegations scheduled for 4pm has had to be called off because the divisions among countries are still to great to be bridged, according to people familiar with the issue, here in Antalya.

Some countries are thought to have seen the full draft of a proposed new final text of the cover decision, while other countries report being shown only segments.

At Cop27 in Sharm El-Sheikh in 2022, the Egyptian presidency drew the ire of dozens of countries on the Saturday (before the talks finally finished early on Sunday morning) when they called delegations individually into their offices to see only partial versions of a new draft text, with no one allowed to remove copies of the draft and no one sure whether other delegates were being shown the same segments of the same draft.

The joint presidencies of Cop31 are starting to come in for similar criticisms of a lack of transparency in these final stages of the negotiations.

With the heads of delegation meeting postponed, it is not known when multiparty negotiations will begin again, after this interlude of shuttle diplomacy with individual nations.

1h ago13.13 GMTAjit NiranjanHello, this is Ajit Niranjan, taking over the blog from my colleague Natalie Hanman. There is plenty to come in the coming hours, and our team on the ground is keeping you covered with the latest.

Updated at 13.43 GMT2h ago12.46 GMTFiona HarveyNot enough attention has been paid at Cop31 to the growing impacts of the El Niño weather system, former Irish president Mary Robinson has warned.

This year’s El Niño is set to be the most powerful on record, and is forecast soon to reach its peak. El Niño is a recurrent weather system in the Pacific, which brings marine heatwaves, disruption to the Indian monsoon, floods in some regions and drought in others. About 50m people could be pushed into severe hunger by El Niño, which has been super-charged by the climate crisis.

“I’m concerned about the super El Niño,” Robinson told the Guardian, speaking before the conference entered overtime. “There isn’t the sense of urgency to address these issues, which actually is present elsewhere, but not here. That to me is very frustrating. Cops should have overall responsibility [for tackling the climate crisis].”

She questioned whether Cop31 was getting enough backing from the highest level of governments around the world.

double quotation mark“We saw that in Paris, there was that momentum and there was leadership from France itself and leadership from [US president Barack] Obama and Xi [Jinping, president of China]. We’re in a much worse position now, and yet we have co-presidents who haven’t really been stepping up and giving that leadership.”

double quotation mark“I’m frustrated by an absence of a real sense of responsibility for how serious the climate and nature crises are, how urgent it is. I’m becoming more of an angry granny when I think about why we are not doing more and why at this Cop we don’t have that sense of a driving urgency.”

She pointed to last year’s Cop30 in Belem, when Brazilian President Lula da Silva attended and pushed for a stronger outcome. “We didn’t get [language in the final text pledging] the phasing out of fossil fuels but we did get the roadmaps [produced by Brazil, for a global fossil fuel phase-out and halt to deforestation],” she said.

Robinson, who was twice a UN climate envoy, as well as serving as UN High Commissioner on Human Rights, and is now taking on the chair of the Global Green Growth Institute, recalled how she had been sent by the UN to Honduras during a previous El Niño in 2016.

double quotation mark“I remember sitting under a tree with women on chairs out in the sun, and an older woman saying to me ‘We have no water’. How do you live without water? There were tears in her eyes. I will just never forget. That’s happening all over the world now – it’s heat, it’s drought, it’s flooding, it’s climate shocks beyond belief. And this El Niño will drive a lot of people into hunger, and destroy homes.”

Cop31 must regain its sense of common humanity, she urged.

Photograph: Graham Readfearn/The GuardianCop negotiations president and Australian climate minister Chris Bowen strides away from a quick meeting with the Fijian climate minister Lynda Tabuya. “How is it going minister,” I asked. “Spectacular,” came the possibly sarcastic answer, with a smile.

2h ago12.14 GMT'We will not allow obstruction to dampen our resolve,' says Tuvalu climate ministerGraham ReadfearnThe Tuvalu climate minister, Dr Maina Talia, has just been speaking to reporters in a very tight huddle in the media centre here.

“My goodness,” he exclaimed as the microphones were thrust within an inch of his face.

But he was here to make a point.

View image in fullscreenTuvalu’s climate minister Maina Talia gives a statement to the media during the first overtime day of Cop31. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images“Every year there seems to be greater discontent, mistrust and frustration from civil society and the countries that are most climate-burdened, vulnerable, and faultless,” he said.

Talia said it was normal for Cop meetings to run into overtime, but then challenged any notion that this was just like previous Cops.

double quotation markYou might say, “We have been here before.” But have we? Have we been here, beyond the 1.5C safety limit in the territory of overshoot?

Have we been beyond the tropical coral reef tipping point? Have we seen thousands buried beneath a Himalayan glacier? Clearly not.”

He said the organised efforts evolving outside the Cop process where countries are lining up with roadmaps to exit from the fossil fuel era “has not given up on the [UN climate convention].”

“The [Transition Away from Fossil Fuels] forum is moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation; governments working together in the spirit of neighbourliness, cooperation and solidarity,” he said.

Tuvalu is due to host the second TAFF meeting next year and he said it would be “a touch point for governments to come together and help each other in building a system free of fossil fuels.”

double quotation markDoes this mean we are happy with the state of the negotiations or accept the lack of ambition we are witnessing because we have an alternate pathway? No. Absolutely not.
